analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to disclose workplace surveillance, restricts how they use worker data, and bans selling it.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in committee when the 118th Congress ended, with only two House Democrats backing it.
analysis.plain_summary: The Stop Spying Bosses Act would require employers with 11 or more workers to tell employees exactly what workplace surveillance they run — what data is collected, how, and how it affects hiring, firing, and pay decisions. It would ban using surveillance to spot union organizing or whistleblowers, block monitoring of workers while off duty or in sensitive areas like restrooms, prohibit selling worker data, and give workers a right to see and correct the data collected on them. It would also create a new Privacy and Technology Division at the Department of Labor to enforce the rules, and let workers and unions sue with statutory damages and without forced arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at covered employers — private firms, state agencies, federal offices, and congressional offices — gain disclosure of every surveillance system watching them, the right to see and correct their own data, and bans on the harshest practices: monitoring off-duty workers, watching restrooms and locker rooms, using surveillance to identify union supporters or whistleblowers, and selling or licensing worker data. Workers hit with an employment decision based on surveillance data could review that data within 7 days. Unions gain the right to sue on workers' behalf, and all workers get protection from retaliation and freedom from forced arbitration for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, job applicants, and labor unions

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to disclose, in plain language, every workplace surveillance system — what data it collects, how and when, where it is stored, and how it feeds decisions about hiring, firing, pay, and promotion — and to get each worker's acknowledgment of receipt.

Bans using surveillance to identify or monitor workers who form or join a union, engage in protected concerted activity, or report the employer's legal violations, and bars collecting political views, health status, disability, or immigration status unrelated to the job.

Prohibits monitoring workers while off duty, in restrooms, locker rooms, lactation or prayer spaces, and any surveillance that threatens mental or physical health; also bans automated systems from predicting worker behavior unrelated to work.
Bans selling or licensing worker data collected through surveillance, and requires a worker's opt-out plus encryption before any transfer of identifying data to a third party.

Gives workers the right to obtain, within 7 days of asking, any data the employer collected on them, and to have incomplete or erroneous data corrected; workers also must be told within 7 days when an employment decision used surveillance data.

Creates a Privacy and Technology Division in the Department of Labor with investigative authority to enforce the rules, prioritizing industries with high surveillance rates, and requires biennial studies of workplace surveillance for Congress.

Protects workers from retaliation for exercising these rights and lets workers and unions sue in federal court with statutory damages (up to $40,000 for prohibited surveillance use, up to $100,000 for retaliation), attorney's fees, and reinstatement for whistleblowers — and voids predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these claims.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more workers bear the cost: building disclosure systems, updating them within 7 days of any change, keeping and preserving compliance records, restricting who on staff can access worker data, and writing compliance terms into every surveillance-vendor contract. Vendors of employee-monitoring software and any third party handling worker data lose the ability to sell or freely transfer it and must follow the same rules, with employers liable if they knew or should have known of a vendor's violation. Taxpayers fund the new Labor Department division and its advisory boards.

drawbacks.text: The 11-employee coverage threshold sweeps in very small businesses, and the compliance load is heavy: detailed disclosures within 30–60 days, updated within 7 days of any change, written acknowledgments, records preservation, and mandatory contract terms with every vendor.

The private right of action with statutory damages — up to $500 per worker for each disclosure failure, $20,000 per violation of the surveillance prohibitions, and $100,000 for retaliation — invites litigation over technical violations even where no worker was harmed.

Key terms are broad: 'workplace surveillance' covers on- and off-duty monitoring, and the ban on automated decision systems that 'predict behavior' and the data-minimization rule barring collection not 'reasonably related to operations' could force changes to ordinary productivity, scheduling, and HR software whose permissible scope would be worked out in regulation and court.

Establishing a new division at the Labor Department, with a Presidentially appointed Administrator, staff hired outside standard pay and hiring rules, and four advisory boards exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act, is a permanent new federal expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are substantial and aimed at practices that are invisible to workers today: covert monitoring, off-duty tracking, union-targeting, and the sale of worker data. The disclosure and data-access rights are the kind of cost that falls mainly on firms already running the surveillance. The real design risks are on the edges — the low 11-employee threshold, broad definitions, and statutory damages could generate compliance and litigation costs disproportionate to harm for some employers, and the new division's structure (hiring and pay outside civil-service rules, FACA-exempt boards) was written for speed rather than oversight. Even granting those objections, the bill's main burden falls on a practice whose costs currently fall entirely on workers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees — Education and the Workforce, Oversight, and House Administration — without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio introduced the bill on March 15, 2024, with Rep. Suzanne Bonamici; it was referred the same day to the Education and the Workforce Committee and, in addition, to the Oversight and Accountability Committee and the House Administration Committee.
Bonamici was the bill's only cosponsor, and no Republican ever signed on; no further action appears in the record after the referrals.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee without any committee or floor vote, as the entire action history consists of the introduction and referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers using workplace surveillance and the vendors that sell monitoring tools are better off: none of the disclosure, data-sale, off-duty-monitoring, or union-surveillance restrictions took effect, and no enforcement division was created.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists; the bill's only two supporters were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill bars them from selling or re-transferring worker data, subjects them to Labor Department investigations, and makes their employer clients liable for violations they should have known about. Their business of monitoring workers off duty or detecting union activity would be directly outlawed.
A flat ban on selling or licensing data collected through workplace surveillance — to any person or, except as required by law, any government entity — cuts off worker data as a tradeable commodity.

Any firm with 11 or more workers would owe detailed surveillance disclosures, 7-day updates, data-access and correction rights for workers, data-minimization limits, and exposure to statutory-damages suits without forced arbitration.
Unions gain standing to sue over surveillance used against organizing or concerted activity, statutory damages, and attorney's fees — a new enforcement tool for protecting members.
